rounds.lieNote: Plausible because 19th-century lotteries offered odd prizes and Sweden has a long coastline full of lighthouses; this lottery never existed.

statements.text: In 1932, the Australian Army sent soldiers armed with Lewis machine guns to cull emus that were damaging wheat farms in Western Australia.
statements.expansion: Farmers who had served in the First World War asked for the machine guns, and the newspapers soon called the operation a war.

statements.text: In 1859, Sweden held a national lottery whose grand prize was a working lighthouse, and it was won by a farmer who had never seen the sea.
The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted somewhere between 38 and 45 minutes, making it the shortest recorded war in history.
statements.expansion: It was fought on the morning of 27 August 1896 after a dispute over who would succeed the sultan of Zanzibar.

rounds.lieNote: Plausible because some animals, like catfish, really do taste through their skin; axolotls do not.

statements.text: The axolotl can taste food through the skin on its tail, which helps it find worms buried in the mud of Mexican lakes.
Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, which they arrange to mark their territory and attract mates.
statements.expansion: The cubic shape is thought to help the droppings stack without rolling away, and studying it won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2019.

statements.text: One rotation of Venus on its axis takes 243 Earth days, which is longer than the 225 days it takes to orbit the Sun.
statements.expansion: Venus also spins in the opposite direction to most planets, including Earth.

rounds.lieNote: Plausible because small Alpine villages really do have unusual addressing rules; this village is invented.

statements.text: Bir Tawil, an area of desert about 2,060 square kilometres on the border between Egypt and Sudan, is claimed by neither country.
statements.expansion: Each country prefers a border line that gives it the neighbouring Halaib Triangle, which is far more valuable.

statements.text: The Belgian municipality of Baarle-Hertog is made up of 26 separate parcels of land, and 22 of them sit entirely inside the Netherlands.
statements.expansion: Some of those Belgian pieces contain small Dutch enclaves of their own.

statements.text: A village in the Swiss Alps has no house numbers at all, because its only street loops back on itself and has no official starting point.

rounds.lieNote: Plausible because early Olympics included many unusual events and demonstration sports; kite flying was never one of them.

statements.text: From 1912 to 1948, the Olympics awarded medals for works of art in painting, music, literature, sculpture and architecture.
statements.expansion: Every entry had to be inspired by sport, and the events were nicknamed the Pentathlon of the Muses.

source.title: Art competitions at the Summer Olympics

statements.text: Tug of war was an Olympic event at every Summer Games from 1900 to 1920 before it was dropped from the program.
statements.expansion: Teams had six pullers in 1900 and eight from 1908 onward.

source.title: Tug of war at the Summer Olympics

statements.text: Competitive kite flying was a demonstration sport at the 1908 London Olympics, judged on the height and steadiness of each kite.

rounds.lieNote: Plausible because early film audiences loved novelty tricks like reversed footage; no cinema ever made it a rule.

statements.text: In 1911, a former Louvre glazier stole the Mona Lisa after blending in with museum staff by wearing one of their white work smocks.
statements.expansion: Vincenzo Peruggia hid the painting in his Paris apartment and was not arrested until December 1913.

statements.text: The first public cinema in Lisbon showed every film twice, once forward and once in reverse, because its audiences demanded it.
John Cage's 1952 piece 4′33″ instructs performers not to play their instruments at all during any of its three movements.
statements.expansion: Its premiere caused shock and led musicologists to question whether the piece counted as music at all.
